storyboard.title: How the Black Death Changed Europe

scenes.narration: In just a few years, the Black Death killed up to half of Europe's people.
scenes.heading: How the Black Death Changed Europe
scenes.subheading: How did the Black Death change Europe?

scenes.narration: It reportedly entered Europe in 1347 when Mongols catapulted infected corpses into Caffa during a siege.
Genoese traders fled on ships, bringing the disease to Sicily by October.
The bacterium Yersinia pestis caused three forms: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic plague.
scenes.text: Yersinia causes three types of plague in humans: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic.

scenes.narration: The massive death toll shattered the labor supply, giving surviving peasants leverage to demand higher wages.
Labor shortage weakened feudal ties and may have helped end feudalism in Europe.
Antisemitism exploded as Jews were blamed, leading to massacres in Strasbourg and Mainz in 1349.
The Black Death killed up to half of Europeans, may have helped end feudalism, sparked anti-Jewish violence, and launched the first public health responses.

facts.text: The Black Death killed up to 50 million people in Europe from 1346 to 1353.
facts.quote: It was one of the most fatal pandemics in human history, leading to the death of up to 50 million people, around 30% to 60% of the European population and approximately 33% of the Middle Eastern population.

facts.text: The pandemic was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis spread by flea bites.
facts.quote: The disease was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is primarily spread by flea bites, though it may also spread through contact with infected tissues or fluids and, in pneumonic cases, through respiratory droplets.

facts.text: The Black Death spread from Alexandria along the African coast to Tunis, then to Morocco via a Moroccan army.
facts.quote: The pandemic spread westwards from Alexandria along the African coast, while in April 1348 Tunis was infected by ship from Sicily. Tunis was then under attack by an army from Morocco; this army dispersed in 1348 and brought the contagion with them to Morocco.

facts.text: Mecca was infected in 1348 by pilgrims returning from the Hajj.
facts.quote: Mecca became infected in 1348 by pilgrims performing the Hajj.

facts.text: The Rasulid sultan of Yemen carried plague back to his homeland after being released from Mamluk captivity in Egypt.
facts.quote: In 1351 or 1352, the Rasulid sultan of the Yemen, al-Mujahid Ali, was released from Mamluk captivity in Egypt and carried plague with him on his return home.

facts.text: In 1349, the cities of Mosul and Baghdad suffered massive epidemics during the ongoing pandemic.
facts.quote: During 1349, records show the city of Mosul suffered a massive epidemic, and the city of Baghdad experienced a second round of the disease.

facts.text: Body lice can transmit the Orientalis biotype of Yersinia pestis
facts.quote: The finding that human body lice can be bubonic plague vectors suggests a mechanism for human-to-human transmission continuing during winter in inland areas and, as suggested by the authors, could also explain total deaths in households.

facts.text: The 2007 study examined teeth from three port cities in France
facts.quote: The 3 locations in that study were all port cities: 2 on the Mediterranean Sea and 1 on the Rhone River

facts.text: The Black Death occurred between 1347 and 1351
facts.quote: none of which were dated to the Black Death era (1347–1351)

facts.text: There is a scientific debate about the cause of medieval European plague epidemics
facts.quote: A scientific debate with public health implications wages: What caused the medieval European plague epidemics known as Black Death?

facts.text: A rat flea-only hypothesis does not fit documented characteristics of Black Death
facts.quote: Recent articles note inconsistencies between a rat flea–borne pandemic of Yersinia pestis (the bacterium that causes bubonic plague) and the documented characteristics of Black Death

facts.text: Europe lost between one third and one half of its population between 1347 and 1351.
facts.quote: Europe suffered an especially significant death toll from the plague. Modern estimates range between roughly one third and one half of the total European population in the five-year period of 1347 to 1351 died during which the most severely-affected areas may have lost up to 80% of the population.

facts.text: The Black Death peaked in Europe between 1348 and 1350, with an estimated third of the population dying.
facts.quote: The Black Death peaked in Europe between 1348 and 1350, with an estimated third of the continent's population ultimately succumbing to the disease.

facts.text: Jean Froissart estimated the death toll to be one-third of the population.
facts.quote: Contemporary chronicler Jean Froissart estimated the toll to be one-third, which modern scholars consider less an accurate assessment than an allusion to the Book of Revelation meant to suggest the scope of the plague.

facts.text: Deaths were not evenly distributed, with some areas losing up to 80% of their population.
facts.quote: the most severely-affected areas may have lost up to 80% of the population.

facts.text: World population declined from 475 million to between 350 and 375 million.
facts.quote: estimate that it reduced the total world population from 475 million to between 350 and 375 million.

facts.text: Population recovery took nearly 80 years in most parts of Europe, and over 150 years in some areas.
facts.quote: In most parts of Europe, it took nearly 80 years for population sizes to recover, and in some areas, it took more than 150 years.

facts.text: Black Death led to the end of feudalism in Europe.
facts.quote: the horrors of Black Death were followed by some positive changes. It turns out that the sudden deaths of millions of people restructured social relationships. The transformations caused by the Black Death might have brought an end to feudalism, the social system of Europe at that time.

facts.text: Labor shortage gave surviving peasants more power.
facts.quote: Fewer people meant fewer peasants to work the fields of feudal lords. This gave more power to the workers who didn’t die.

facts.text: Surviving workers saw higher wages.
facts.quote: Soon, workers in cities and in rural areas started to demand higher wages. Wages in England, for example, rose as much as 40 percent between 1340 and 1360.

facts.text: Better living conditions and longer life expectancies after the plague.
facts.quote: The result was a higher standard of living and longer life expectancies for Europeans who survived the plague.

facts.text: Black Death was caused by Yersinia bacteria and resulted in three plague forms: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic.
facts.quote: Yersinia causes three types of plague in humans: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic.

facts.text: Bubonic plague symptoms included fever, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes (buboes), and delirium.
facts.quote: It also causes buboes: one or more of the lymph nodes become tender and swollen, usually in the groin or armpits.

facts.text: Pneumonic plague affected the lungs and caused severe pneumonia-like symptoms including shortness of breath and fluid in the lungs.
facts.quote: Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and causes symptoms similar to those of severe pneumonia: fever, weakness, and shortness of breath.

facts.text: Septicemic plague was a blood infection causing fever, fatigue, and internal bleeding.
facts.quote: Septicemic plague is an infection of the blood. Its symptoms include fatigue, fever, and internal bleeding.

facts.text: Most victims likely experienced a combination of the three plague forms during the Black Death pandemic.
facts.quote: Although there is DNA evidence that Yersinia was present in victims of the Black Death, it is uncertain which form the majority of the infection took. It is likely that all three played some role in the pandemic.

facts.text: Black Death victims suffered additional symptoms such as vomiting, headaches, light intolerance, back pain, and sleeplessness.
facts.quote: Bubonic plague causes fever, fatigue, shivering, vomiting, headaches, giddiness, intolerance to light, pain in the back and limbs, sleeplessness, apathy, and delirium.

facts.text: Vikings halted exploration due to plague in 1349
facts.quote: July, 1349 An English ship brings the Black Death to Norway when it runs aground in Bergen. The ship’s crew is dead by the end of the week and the pestilence travels to Denmark and Sweden, where the king believes fasting on a Friday and foregoing shoes on Sunday will please God and end the plague.

facts.text: Plague reached London in 1348 after Princess Joan's death
facts.quote: March, 1350 [...] October, 1348 Following the infection and death of King Edward III’s daughter Princess Joan, the plague reaches London, according to King Death: by Colin Platt.

facts.text: Jewish massacres occurred in Strasbourg and Mainz in 1349
facts.quote: February, 1349 One of the worst massacres of Jews during the Black Death takes place on Valentine’s Day in Strasbourg, with 2,000 Jewish people burned alive. In the spring, 3,000 Jews defend themselves in Mainz against Christians but are overcome and slaughtered.

facts.text: Plague killed 100,000 people in Wales in 1349
facts.quote: April, 1349 The plague hits Wales, brought by people fleeing from Southern England, and eventually kills100,000 people there.

facts.text: Venice implemented early pandemic response measures in 1348
facts.quote: Venice faces its own outbreak by pioneering the first organized response, with committees ordering ship inspections and burning those with contagions, shutting down taverns, and restricting wine from unknown sources.

facts.text: Plague entered England through Melcombe Regis in June 1348
facts.quote: June, 1348 The plague enters England through the port of Melcombe Regis, in Dorset. As it spreads through the town, some escape by fleeing inland, inadvertently spreading it further.

facts.text: The Black Death killed an estimated one-third of Europe's population in the 14th century.
facts.quote: killing an estimated one-third of Europe’s population in the 14th century

facts.text: The plague spread rapidly along trade routes and killed an estimated 25 million people in Europe.
facts.quote: The disease spread rapidly along trade routes and ultimately killed an estimated one-fourth to one-third of the total population of Europe, or 25 million people

facts.text: Labor shortages after the plague weakened the feudal system and changed worker-landowner relationships.
facts.quote: labor shortages that weakened the feudal system and altered relationships between workers and landowners

facts.text: Antisemitism intensified as Jews were blamed for the Black Death, leading to violent pogroms and mass killings.
facts.quote: Antisemitism greatly intensified throughout Europe as Jews were blamed for the spread of the Black Death. A wave of violent pogroms ensued, and entire Jewish communities were killed by mobs or burned at the stake en masse

facts.text: The Black Death led to early forms of quarantine and disease control practices.
facts.quote: leading to early forms of quarantine and disease control

facts.text: In Siena, the plague caused population loss that stopped cathedral enlargement and ended the Sienese school of painting.
facts.quote: The economy of Siena received a decisive check. The city’s population was so diminished that the project of enlarging the cathedral was abandoned, and the death of many great painters, such as Ambrogio and Pietro Lorenzetti, brought the development of the first Sienese school to a premature end

facts.text: The Black Death first arrived in Europe via Mongol siege of Caffa in 1347
facts.quote: It was reportedly first introduced to Europe when Mongols lobbed plague-infected corpses during the siege of Caffa in the Crimea in 1347.

facts.text: Genoese traders fled Caffa and brought plague to Sicily in October 1347
facts.quote: In October 1347, a fleet of Genoese trading ships fleeing Caffa reached the port of Messina in Sicily.

facts.text: All crew members on the fleeing ships were infected or dead upon reaching Messina
facts.quote: By the time the fleet reached Messina, all the crew members were either infected or dead.

facts.text: Plague spread from Sicily to Italian cities Genoa and Venice by late 1347–early 1348
facts.quote: From there, the plague spread to Genoa and Venice by the turn of 1347–1348, spreading across Italy.

facts.text: Mongols catapulted plague-infected corpses into Caffa during a 1345 siege
facts.quote: In 1345 the Mongols under Khan Jani Beg of the Golden Horde besieged Caffa. Suffering from an outbreak of black plague, the Mongols placed plague-infected corpses in catapults and threw them into the city.

facts.text: The Silk Road spread theory is disputed due to Pax Mongolica breakdown by 1325
facts.quote: However even the Silk Road spread theory is disputed, as others point out that the Pax Mongolica had already broken down by 1325, when Western and Persian traders found it difficult to conduct trade in the region

facts.text: Black Death originated in China and Central Asia during the 14th century
facts.quote: The epidemic of the 14th century originated in China and Central Asia.

facts.text: Disease spread to Europe via siege at Kaffa in 1347
facts.quote: It was transmitted to Europe in 1347, when a Eurasian army besieged the Genoese trading post of Kaffa in the Crimean Peninsula.

facts.text: Genoese ships carried plague from Kaffa to Mediterranean ports
facts.quote: From Kaffa, Genoese ships carried the disease westward to Mediterranean ports.

facts.text: Plague reached Sicily in 1347 and spread to Europe in following years
facts.quote: Plague reached Sicily in 1347; North Africa, mainland Italy, Spain, England, and France in 1348.

facts.text: Black Death spread across Europe by 1350 reaching Scandinavia and Baltic lands
facts.quote: and from there it spread inland. Plague reached Sicily in 1347; North Africa, mainland Italy, Spain, England, and France in 1348; Austria, Hungary, Switzerland, Germany, and the Low Countries in 1349; and Scandinavia and the Baltic lands in 1350.

facts.text: Recurring plague outbreaks occurred in Europe between 1361 and 1400
facts.quote: There were recurrences of plague in 1361–63, 1369–71, 1374–75, 1390, and 1400.
